lesson.title: Bulimia Nervosa: Inside the Binge-Purge Cycle
lesson.summary: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent episodes of binge eating paired with compensatory behaviors like vomiting, laxative misuse, or excessive exercise, occurring at least weekly for three months, with self-evaluation unduly tied to body shape and weight.
lesson.body:
Bulimia nervosa shares its category with anorexia nervosa but has a distinct clinical picture. It is defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating, meaning eating, within a discrete period of time, an amount of food that is clearly larger than most people would eat under similar circumstances, combined with a felt sense of lack of control over the eating during that episode. It also requires recurrent inappropriate compensatory behavior aimed at preventing weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives or diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise. Both the binge eating and the compensatory behavior must occur, on average, at least once a week for three months, and self-evaluation must be unduly influenced by body shape and weight. The diagnosis does not apply if the pattern occurs exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa, since anorexia's binge-eating/purging subtype takes precedence in that case.

A clinically important distinguishing feature is that body weight in bulimia nervosa is typically within or above the normal range, unlike the significantly low weight required for anorexia nervosa. This matters practically: someone can be dealing with a serious, sometimes life-threatening eating disorder while appearing, by weight alone, unremarkable to family, friends, or even physicians. That is part of why bulimia nervosa often goes unrecognized longer than anorexia nervosa, since it does not carry the same visible physical signs.

The binge-purge pattern tends to function as a self-perpetuating cycle. Binges are often preceded by restrictive eating or by a difficult emotional state, such as stress, shame, or low mood. The binge itself can bring brief relief or numbing, but it is quickly followed by intense guilt and fear of weight gain, which drives the compensatory behavior. That compensatory behavior, in turn, tends to increase physical deprivation and emotional distress, setting the stage for the next binge. Understanding this as a cycle, rather than as isolated moments of poor judgment, is important both for reducing shame and for designing treatment that interrupts the cycle at more than one point.

The medical complications of bulimia nervosa differ from those of anorexia nervosa because they center on the effects of purging rather than starvation alone. Repeated vomiting and laxative or diuretic misuse can cause electrolyte imbalances, particularly involving potassium, which can lead to dangerous cardiac arrhythmias. Repeated vomiting can also cause esophageal irritation or tearing, dental erosion from stomach acid, and swelling of the salivary glands. These are genuinely serious medical risks, not incidental side effects.

As with anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa involves a disruption of the normal hunger and satiety system covered in earlier chapters, though the disruption runs in a different direction: binge eating overrides the body's normal satiety signals, while purging overrides the body's normal drive to retain the calories that were consumed. Framing bulimia nervosa this way, as a disorder with a specific clinical profile and a real medical footprint, helps counter the common and inaccurate view of it as simply overeating followed by regret.
